conflicts.description: Public solenoid 17, the first continuous output, is asserted continuously by the ROM but is not one of the three continuous devices the solenoid identification table lists. PinMAME's LISY bridge treats Centaur's continuous bit 0 as a strobe line and masks it out of the coil data, while by35.c takes the sixth switch-column strobe from PIA1:B bit 7 (public 20) instead. The two readings cannot both be right and the address stays unresolved.

PIA1:B bit 4, the first of the four continuous outputs, and the one continuous output the solenoid identification table does not account for: the table lists exactly three continuous devices, at printed 16, 17 and 18, which are public 18, 19 and 20. What public 17 does on Centaur is unresolved and the two available sources disagree. The ROM asserts it and never releases it - in the retained self-test trace it goes high once and is still high in the final snapshot - so it is a driven line and not an empty slot. PinMAME's LISY bridge special-cases Centaur at src/lisy/lisy35.c case 7, setting lisy35_J4PIN5_is_strobe, after which lisy35_solenoid_handler masks continuous bit 0 out of the coil data with cont_data &= 0x0e, i.e. it treats this line as a strobe rather than a coil. But by35.c assembles the sixth switch column for non-Vector games from PIA1:B bit 7, which is public 20, the magnet, not bit 4. Until that is reconciled the address stays unknown rather than being asserted either as unused or as the column strobe.

Solenoid identification table entry 16. The ROM's own solenoid self test pulses this coil while displaying 16, which printed page 13 states is the number assigned to the solenoid, so public address 18 and printed number 16 are the same device. The retained v2.0.0 script repurposes this address to drive desktop and VR backglass illumination; that is a table convenience, not the physical device.

Solenoid identification table entry 17. The ROM's own solenoid self test pulses this coil while displaying 17, which printed page 13 states is the number assigned to the solenoid, so public address 19 and printed number 17 are the same device. Energising this relay enables the two flipper coils, which are wired through it rather than to a driver-board output and therefore have no solenoid number of their own. The retained standalone script uses it as the game-on signal for nudge handling.
